lesson.title: Build a grouped report

lead.text: GROUP BY item gathers orders with the same item. Each group becomes one result row, and SUM works inside the group.
WHERE filters rows before the groups are made. HAVING filters groups after their totals exist.

steps.headline: GROUP BY makes each result row stand for a group, and HAVING filters the groups.

lead.text: Several orders share an item. Group them, and the report's rows stand for something new.

reveal.text: You counted the different items. The report now has one row per item instead of one per order.

queries.label: Group by item
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Group by status
queries.sql: SELECT status, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

steps.headline: Report each status with its orders, known amounts and total.

queries.label: Counts by status
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

queries.label: With totals
queries.sql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

workedSteps.text: Count rows and known amounts in each group.
Add the known amounts in each group.

lead.text: Inside a group, COUNT(amount) counts only that group's known amounts.

reveal.text: You counted inside one group. A grouped report can show both counts, so incomplete groups stand out.

queries.label: Order counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Known amount counts
queries.sql: SELECT item, COUNT(*) AS orders, COUNT(amount) AS known_amounts FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

lead.text: WHERE works on single rows, before any groups exist. A group's total exists only once the groups are made.

reveal.text: You named the clause that tests finished groups. Keep the row filter and the group filter apart in your head.

queries.label: Total at least 100
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Total at least 200
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 200 ORDER BY item;

lead.text: Filter the rows first, then group what is left. Read the row filter and the group filter separately.

queries.label: Every status
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY item ORDER BY item;

queries.label: Paid total at least 50
queries.sql: SELECT item, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY item HAVING SUM(amount) >= 50 ORDER BY item;

lesson.orientation: Build a report whose rows represent groups, then filter its calculated totals.
lesson.nextAction: Apply the idea to the next query.

blocks.text: A café keeps slips: tea £2, coffee £3, tea £4, coffee £1 and tea £1.

intro.promise: By the end you'll build a report with one row per group, and filter rows before grouping or groups afterwards.

recap.keyIdea: GROUP BY makes each result row a group. WHERE filters rows before grouping, and HAVING filters the totals afterwards.

blocks.text: You grouped orders into 3 items and counted 1 known Lamp amount. A paid Desk total came to 160.

recap.nextHook: Next, bring two tables together with a join.

questions.prompt: How many result rows does GROUP BY item produce?
hints: Identify different item names.
One result row represents one item group.
The groups are Book, Desk and Lamp; each gets a result row.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are three item groups: Book, Desk and Lamp.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Each different item becomes one result row, so the rows now stand for items.

misconceptions.feedback: That is one row per order. GROUP BY gathers orders that share an item.
That counts the statuses. Count the different item names.

questions.prompt: Within the Lamp group, what is COUNT(amount)?
hints: COUNT(column) counts known values.
Compare the two Lamp amount cells.
In the Lamp group, order 104 has an amount and order 106 has NULL. Count only the known cell.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only order 104 has a known Lamp amount; order 106 is NULL.

questions.onCorrect: 1. COUNT(amount) counts only the known amounts inside the group.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts both Lamp rows. COUNT(amount) skips the unknown amount.

questions.prompt: Name the SQL clause that can filter groups on SUM(amount).
hints: The total exists after the rows are grouped.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, so it can test SUM(amount). WHERE filters the input rows before their group totals are computed.

questions.onCorrect: HAVING. A group total exists only after grouping, and HAVING tests groups.

misconceptions.feedback: WHERE sees single rows before they are grouped, so the total does not exist yet.
GROUP BY makes the groups. Something else has to test their totals.

questions.prompt: After WHERE status = 'paid', what is the Desk group's SUM(amount)?
hints: Keep only paid Desk orders.
Add the two eligible amounts.
Evaluate 80 + 80 for the eligible Desk orders.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Paid Desk orders 101 and 103 have amounts 80 and 80; their total is 160.

questions.onCorrect: 160. WHERE keeps the paid rows, then the Desk group adds its two amounts.

misconceptions.feedback: Both paid Desk orders count. Add them.
That is the total of all paid orders. The question is about Desk only.

questions.prompt: How many item groups survive HAVING SUM(amount) >= 40 in the original data?
hints: Compute each group total first.
The threshold includes totals equal to forty.
The totals are Book 40, Desk 160 and Lamp 40; test each with >= 40.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Book is 40, Desk is 160 and Lamp is 40. All three meet the inclusive threshold.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Each group total is tested, and totals equal to the threshold pass.

misconceptions.feedback: Totals equal to the threshold pass, because >= keeps them.
Several groups reach the threshold exactly, and >= keeps those.

questions.prompt: What does WHERE status = 'paid' change in a grouped query?
hints: WHERE defines the rows supplied to the groups.

acceptedIdeas: It filters individual rows before grouping
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: WHERE retains only paid input rows before grouping. Group counts and totals are calculated from that filtered set.

choices.label: It filters individual rows before grouping

questions.onCorrect: It filters individual rows before grouping. The groups are built from what remains.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a job for a later clause. WHERE acts before any totals exist.
WHERE never renames anything. It keeps or drops rows.

questions.prompt: How much did tea sell for in total?
hints: Which slips are about tea?
Put the tea slips together.
Add only the tea slips.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The tea slips are £2, £4 and £1, which add up to £7.

questions.onCorrect: 7. You gathered the slips by drink and added within each pile. GROUP BY and SUM do the same.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds every slip. The question is about tea only.

questions.prompt: In a grouped report, one result row stands for what?
hints: Think about what GROUP BY gathers.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GROUP BY gathers rows that share a value, and each gathered set becomes one result row.

questions.onCorrect: Each result row of a grouped report stands for a whole group of input rows.

misconceptions.feedback: Grouping gathers several rows together, so a result row stands for many.
Columns are the facts shown. Rows are what the report counts.

questions.prompt: Why does the pending group show fewer known amounts than orders?
hints: Compare COUNT(*) with COUNT(amount) for the group.

acceptedIdeas: One pending order has no recorded amount.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: COUNT(*) counts both pending orders. COUNT(amount) skips the one whose amount is unknown.

questions.onCorrect: COUNT(*) counts orders and COUNT(amount) counts known amounts, so an unknown amount makes them differ.

choices.label: One pending order has no recorded amount.
Pending orders are not counted at all.

misconceptions.feedback: COUNT(*) counts every row in the group, whatever its values.
Both pending orders are counted in the orders column.

questions.prompt: The rows are tea (paid) 3, tea (pending) 5 and coffee (paid) 4. After WHERE status = 'paid' and GROUP BY item, what is tea's SUM?
hints: Which rows does WHERE keep?
The pending row is dropped before grouping.
Tea has one paid row left.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: WHERE removes the pending tea row first, so tea's group holds only the paid 3.

questions.onCorrect: 3. WHERE drops rows before the groups are made, so the dropped row never reaches the total.

misconceptions.feedback: That includes the pending row. WHERE removes it before grouping.
